# Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling

Fangcong Yin Affiliation: Meta    Ming Yin Affiliation: Meta
Affiliation: Duke University    Tanvi Bhandarkar Affiliation: Meta   
Aashu Singh Affiliation: Meta    Eryk Helenowski Affiliation: Meta   
Shlok Kumar Mishra Affiliation: Meta    Saghar Hosseini
Affiliation: Meta    Karthik Abinav Sankararaman Affiliation: Meta   
Greg Durrett Affiliation: New York University    Dinkar Juyal
Affiliation: Meta

###### Abstract

LLM agents are commonly trained with RLVR, but the sparse nature of
typical RLVR rewards makes credit assignment challenging, especially for
long-horizon tasks. We propose Self-Credit, an end-to-end agentic RL
method that creates dense supervision signals from sparse outcome
rewards using self-generated credit assignment via intra-group
rescaling. Self-Credit builds on group-based RL with three components.
First, during its rollouts, the policy model generates summaries with
citations to earlier turns containing critical evidence, which serve as
self-generated credit. Second, we refine this model-generated credit
with _intra-group rescaling_, which compares cited actions across
successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt. This approach uses
group-level agreement and disagreement to remove undeserved credit and
further emphasize credit assigned to critical actions. Third, _advantage
reweighting_ uses the rescaled credit weights to update the advantages
of the cited turns. On BrowseComp-Plus, Self-Credit improves over the
base models by $`37.0`$ and $`36.2`$ points on Qwen3 8B and 32B
respectively, and outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines by
$`8.5`$ and $`5.6`$ points, respectively. Self-Credit also improves over
the strongest baselines by $`4.9`$ points on GAIA and $`4.7`$ points on
xBench-DeepSearch. Analyses show that self-generated credit provides
useful signals for selecting critical actions, and that intra-group
rescaling, especially on failed rollouts, is important across model
scales.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2610.28388v1/self-cite-teaser-editable_v4.png)

Figure 1: Self-Credit leverages self-generated summaries with
Intra-group rescaling to provide credit assignment for long-horizon
agentic RL. Self-Credit outperforms strong baselines on challenging
long-horizon tasks, such as BrowseComp-Plus.

Large language models (LLMs) are commonly used for agentic tasks, where
they interact with environments and issue tool calls as actions. A
principal challenge in building long-horizon agents is the nature of
supervision: typically, models are trained via RLVR using only sparse
rewards ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)), as additional dense
supervision is expensive to define and collect ([Tao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19); [Setlur et al., 2025](#bib.bib17); [Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib14); [Zhang et al., 2025e](#bib.bib13)). Recent work
extends standard RLVR algorithms to provide credit assignment even when
only sparse rewards are available, including approaches that use
external judges ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib51); [Zeng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib36)) and learned critics ([Zhang et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib35); [Shi et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)). However, these
methods usually require additional supervision signals and often suffer
from context growth in challenging long-horizon tasks ([Sun et al.,
2025](#bib.bib33)).

Inspired by context management methods for LLM agents ([Li et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib47); [Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)), we propose
Self-Credit, a novel agentic RL method in which the policy LLM agent
performs credit assignment through compaction using self-generated
credit with intra-group rescaling. As illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling"),
Self-Credit builds on a standard group-based RL algorithm with three
components to create dense supervision signals from a single sparse
outcome reward. First, we prompt the policy model to generate a summary
with citations that identify earlier turns in the interaction history
containing critical evidence for the agentic task. The summaries are
used for compaction to compress the long context, and the citations
serve as self-generated credit. Second, _intra-group rescaling_ refines
this credit by comparing cited actions across successful and failed
rollouts for the same prompt. In particular, this rescaling uses
agreement and disagreement across the entire rollout group to determine
how to remove undeserved credit and further emphasize credit assigned to
critical actions, grounding the credit weights in group-level
statistics. Third, _advantage reweighting_ uses the rescaled credit
weights to selectively strengthen the advantages of tokens in
model-cited turns to emphasize important behaviors in a long trajectory.

We evaluate Self-Credit on challenging long-horizon search and retrieval
tasks, including multi-hop QA on BrowseComp-Plus and deep research on
GAIA and xBench-DeepSearch. As shown in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling"),
on BrowseComp-Plus, Self-Credit improves over the Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B
base agents by $`37.0`$ and $`36.2`$ percentage points, respectively,
and outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines by $`8.5`$ and
$`5.6`$ points, respectively. On deep research tasks, Self-Credit also
outperforms the strongest evaluated baselines by $`4.9`$ points on GAIA
and $`4.7`$ points on xBench-DeepSearch.

Ablations show that intra-group credit rescaling, especially
downweighting repeated turns shared across failed rollouts, is important
across model scales, and that using self-generated credit provides more
effective credit assignment than the alternatives. Further analyses show
that self-generated citations identify important actions related to gold
answers, and that intra-group rescaling rules are applied selectively
during training at a higher selection quality than baselines.

Our main contributions are as follows: (1) We introduce Self-Credit, an
end-to-end RL algorithm for training long-horizon agents using
self-generated summaries for turn-level credit assignment with
intra-group rescaling. (2) We propose a novel intra-group credit
rescaling method that refines self-generated credit using both
successful and failed rollouts. (3) We show that Self-Credit outperforms
strong agentic RL baselines on long-horizon agentic tasks across
multiple models at different scales.

## 2 Preliminaries

Long-horizon agentic tasks. We formulate long-horizon tasks for LLM
agents as follows. Given a query $`Q`$, an LLM agent $`M_{\theta}`$
interacts with an environment $`\mathcal{E}`$ and answers $`Q`$ by
taking a sequence of actions over $`T`$ interaction turns, followed by a
final-answer turn. At each interaction turn $`t\in\{0,\dots,T-1\}`$, the
model generates a thinking trace $`I_{t}`$, takes an action
$`a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}`$, and receives an observation
$`o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}`$ from the environment. The agent’s state is
$`s_{t}=(Q,\mathcal{H}_{t})`$, where
$`\mathcal{H}_{t}=\mathcal{H}_{0:t}`$ and
$`\mathcal{H}_{k:t}=((I_{k},a_{k},o_{k}),\dots,(I_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t-1}))`$
for $`k\in\{0,\dots,t\}`$, with $`\mathcal{H}_{t:t}`$ denoting the empty
history. For example, in a tool-use setting, the model takes an action
by issuing a call to an external tool with appropriate parameters. At
the final turn $`t=T`$, the model generates a thinking trace $`I_{T}`$
and a final answer $`a_{T}`$, then terminates the interaction. The
complete trajectory of $`T+1`$ turns is
$`\mathcal{T}=((I_{0},a_{0},o_{0}),\dots,(I_{T-1},a_{T-1},o_{T-1}),(I_{T},a_{T}))`$,
which receives a binary reward $`R(a_{T},Q)`$, abbreviated as
$`R\in\{0,1\}`$.

Multi-turn RL with GRPO. We use GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib40))
to train the model in this multi-turn RL setting. At each training step,
the rollout policy $`M_{\theta}`$ generates $`G`$ trajectories
$`\{\mathcal{T}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}`$ for the same query $`Q`$ through
interactions with the environment, each receiving a reward $`R^{j}`$.
Let $`\widehat{A}^{\,j}`$ denote the advantage for trajectory
$`\mathcal{T}^{j}`$; its detailed formulation can be found in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Formulation Details ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").

Let
$`\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}=((I^{j}_{0},a^{j}_{0}),\dots,(I^{j}_{T^{j}},a^{j}_{T^{j}}))`$
denote the sequence of model-generated thinking traces and actions,
including the final answer, in trajectory $`\mathcal{T}^{j}`$, where
$`T^{j}`$ is its number of interaction turns. We use
$`|\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}|`$ to denote the total number of
model-generated tokens in this sequence. The advantage
$`\widehat{A}^{\,j}`$ is uniformly applied to every token in
$`\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}`$. Further details can be found in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Formulation Details ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").

Credit assignment. GRPO with only outcome rewards provides coarse credit
for a multi-turn decision chain. As the advantage $`\widehat{A}^{\,j}`$
is broadcast uniformly to every model-generated token in the rollout,
all turns share the same advantage. Such reward sparsity becomes more
problematic for long-horizon agentic tasks as the trajectory length
grows, because a single outcome reward must supervise more turns ([Feng
et al., 2025](#bib.bib58); [Zhang, 2026](#bib.bib38)). Providing better
learning signals requires credit assignment, usually expressed through
non-uniform advantage estimates. In this work, we focus on turn-level
advantages $`\widehat{A}^{j}_{t}`$.

Figure 2: Illustration of Self-Credit. (1) Self-Credit leverages
self-compaction with turn citations for credit assignment. (2) Across
rollouts for the same prompt, intra-group rescaling removes extra credit
from cited turns that appear in both successful and failed rollouts,
strengthens positive credit for turns unique to successes, and assigns
stronger negative credit to turns that are only cited by failures. (3)
The rescaled weights are used for advantage reweighting.

## 3 Methods

We present an approach that creates dense supervision signals from
outcome rewards for long-horizon agentic RL using self-generated credit
with intra-group rescaling via compaction. Our method, Self-Credit,
combines three components: (1) the policy performs compaction by
generating summaries of the interaction history, and the summaries cite
important turns in the history as credit; (2) Intra-group rescaling
refines this self-generated credit against the outcomes of other
rollouts for the same prompt; (3) The rescaled credit is used to
upweight the advantages of cited turns.
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
illustrates Self-Credit.

### 3.1 Self-Compaction with Turn Citations

Compaction-augmented RL. Prior work introduces _compaction_ into RLVR
for long-horizon agentic tasks to address issues caused by growing
context ([Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib47); [Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib48);
[Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)). Compaction replaces the interaction
history in the context with a shorter summary, allowing generation to
continue conditioned on the query and summary.

During training, compaction is triggered whenever the context reaches or
exceeds $`C`$ tokens at turn $`t`$, where $`C`$ is a threshold chosen
according to the effective context size of the LLM agent. When
compaction is triggered, a summarizer $`M_{\phi}`$ produces a compact
history $`z_{t}`$ from the current interaction context:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_{t^{\prime}:t}:=\begin{cases}\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t},&|(Q,\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t})|<C,\\
z_{t},\quad z_{t}\sim M_{\phi}(\cdot\mid Q,\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t}),&|(Q,\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t})|\geq C.\end{cases}
``` |  | (1) |

Here, $`t^{\prime}`$ is the most recent turn at which compaction was
triggered before turn $`t`$ ($`t^{\prime}=0`$ if no compaction has been
triggered yet), $`\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t}`$ is the context before
compaction, and $`|(Q,\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t})|`$ denotes the context
length. $`\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_{t^{\prime}:t}`$ is the context after
compaction: the previous interaction context is discarded and replaced
by the summary; the model continues from the query and summary.

Compaction may be triggered multiple times as the context grows again
after each summary. Let $`N^{j}`$ be the number of context-replacing
summaries generated in trajectory $`\mathcal{T}^{j}`$. The trajectory is
then divided into $`N^{j}+1`$ *segments*
$`\{\mathcal{S}_{i}^{j}\}_{i=1}^{N^{j}+1}`$, each conditioned on the
query and the preceding summary if exists.

Following compaction-augmented policy optimization methods such as SUPO
([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)), we extend the GRPO objective to:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{SUM-RL}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\Biggl[\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{G}|\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}|}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\sum_{i=1}^{N^{j}+1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|\mathcal{S}^{j}_{i,M_{\theta}}|}\min\Bigl(\rho^{j}_{i,\ell}\widehat{A}^{\,j},\;\clip\bigl(\rho^{j}_{i,\ell},1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\bigr)\widehat{A}^{\,j}\Bigr)\Biggr],
``` |  | (2) |

where $`\mathcal{S}^{j}_{i,M_{\theta}}`$ contains the trainable
model-generated tokens of segment $`i`$.

Here, $`\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}`$ includes all trainable
policy-generated tokens in the rollout, including summary tokens, so
$`|\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}|=\sum_{i=1}^{N^{j}+1}|\mathcal{S}^{j}_{i,M_{\theta}}|`$.
In other words, the objective computes one advantage per complete
rollout trajectory and broadcasts it across the trainable tokens of all
segments.

Summary with citations. Following [Lu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib41); [Li et
al. (2026b)](#bib.bib47); [Cursor Research et al. (2026)](#bib.bib46),
we use the policy model itself as the summarizer:
$`M_{\phi}=M_{\theta}`$. During training and inference, when compaction
is triggered, we prompt the policy model to summarize important
information in the interaction history and cite important turns using
their indices, producing a citation set
$`K\subseteq\{t^{\prime},\dots,t-1\}`$. During training, the model is
penalized for generating an invalid summary or citation to enforce the
required format. We also prompt the model to provide citations at the
end of the rollout to obtain signals for the final segment. Details of
the prompt and required format can be found in
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Prompts and Instructions ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").

### 3.2 Intra-group Rescaling

However, relying solely on self-generated credit or rewards can
reinforce undesired behaviors; related work shows that optimizing
model-generated feedback can lead to hacking and instability ([Shafayat
et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib31); [Wang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib30); [Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib6)). For example,
instead of selectively citing important turns, the model can cite every
turn in the context. Using such citations for credit assignment would
then fail to provide selective learning signals.

To elicit better learning signals from self-generated citations,
Self-Credit uses information already available in group-based RL without
additional supervision or inference. For a given turn in a rollout, we
examine similar turns across other rollouts in the same prompt group. A
turn that appears more frequently across successful rollouts is more
likely to be associated with success, and the same reasoning applies to
failure. This provides within-group evidence for validating and refining
the model’s self-generated credit.

Given a query $`Q`$ and its group of $`G`$ rollout trajectories
$`\{\mathcal{T}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}`$, let $`\mathcal{C}`$ and
$`\mathcal{F}`$ be the sets of successful and failed rollouts,
respectively. Let $`B_{t}^{j}`$ denote the $`t`$-th turn of trajectory
$`\mathcal{T}^{j}`$. Following [Feng et al. (2025)](#bib.bib58), we
assume that some turns appear more than once and can be matched across
rollouts. For example, in search-agent tasks, two search actions can be
matched if the sets of documents they retrieve have substantial overlap.
In addition, we assume that different turns in a rollout contribute
independently to the final outcome. Details of the matching procedure
and a discussion of this assumption are provided in
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Turn Matching ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").

Let $`n_{+}(B_{t}^{j})`$ and $`n_{-}(B_{t}^{j})`$ denote the numbers of
successful and failed rollouts, respectively, in the group that cite a
turn matching $`B_{t}^{j}`$. Both numbers take the current rollout
$`\mathcal{T}^{j}`$ into consideration. We use these counts to
distinguish the following three critical scenarios for a cited turn: (1)
Repeated success: a matching turn is cited by at least $`\tau_{+}`$
successful rollouts and no failed rollouts; (2) Repeated failure: a
matching turn is cited by at least $`\tau_{-}`$ failed rollouts and no
successful rollouts; and (3) Mixed outcomes: a matching turn is cited by
at least one successful rollout and at least one failed rollout.

Then, for a cited turn $`B_{t}^{j}`$ with $`\widehat{A}^{\,j}\neq 0`$,
we assign a scaling weight as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
w_{t}^{j}:=\begin{cases}w_{s}&\widehat{A}^{\,j}>0,\ n_{-}(B_{t}^{j})=0,\ \text{and }n_{+}(B_{t}^{j})\geq\tau_{+}\quad\text{\footnotesize\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}(Successes)}\\[1.0pt]
1&\widehat{A}^{\,j}>0\ \text{and }n_{-}(B_{t}^{j})>0\quad\text{\footnotesize\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}(Mixed)}\\[2.0pt]
\beta&\widehat{A}^{\,j}>0,\ \text{otherwise}\quad\text{\footnotesize\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}(Base credit)}\\[2.0pt]
w_{f}&\widehat{A}^{\,j}<0,\ n_{+}(B_{t}^{j})=0,\ \text{and }n_{-}(B_{t}^{j})\geq\tau_{-}\quad\text{\footnotesize\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}(Failures)}\\[2.0pt]
1&\widehat{A}^{\,j}<0,\ \text{otherwise}.\\
\end{cases}
``` |  | (3) |

In other words, we refine credit assignment in these three scenarios
through intra-group comparisons: (1) Repeated success: we apply a larger
scaling weight $`w_{s}>\beta`$ to strengthen positive credit; (2)
Repeated failure: we apply a scaling weight $`w_{f}\geq 1`$ to
strengthen the negative advantage; and (3) Mixed outcomes: we remove the
$`\beta`$ upweighting for successful rollouts because the effect of the
cited turn is uncertain. For all other cited turns, we retain the base
weight of $`\beta`$ for positive advantages and $`1`$ for negative
advantages. For uncited turns $`t\notin K`$, we do not change the
advantages, so $`w^{j}_{t}=1`$. The three scenarios are illustrated in
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Preliminaries ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").

Intra-group rescaling is applied only to turns that can be matched
across rollouts. Summary turns and final-answer turns are excluded from
comparisons to preserve credit for summarization and answer commitment.
Nonetheless, we show empirically in
Section [6](#S6 "6 Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
that rescaling can still be triggered frequently, as most agentic
actions within a group are similar when conditioned on the same query.

### 3.3 Advantage Reweighting

We leverage the rescaled weights for advantage reweighting. We use the
citation set to replace the uniform advantage broadcast in
Equation [2](#S3.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 3.1 Self-Compaction with Turn Citations ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
with turn-level weights. For each model-generated token $`\ell`$ in turn
$`t`$ of trajectory $`\mathcal{T}^{j}`$, the token-level advantage is
defined as follows:

|     |                                                          |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widehat{A}^{j}_{t,\ell}:=\widehat{A}^{\,j}\,w^{\,j}_{t}
       ```                                                       |     | (4) |

In other words, all tokens in the same turn receive the same reweighted
advantage using the assigned rescaled weight. In addition, in a
successful rollout trajectory, summary turns and the final-answer turn
are automatically treated as cited so that they receive credit without
requiring explicit citations from the model.

### 3.4 Annealing the Weights

The importance of exploration and exploitation varies across different
stages of LLM post-training ([Cui et al., 2025](#bib.bib29); [Cheng et
al., 2025](#bib.bib28)). Since the rescaled weights can influence this
balance, we design a learning curriculum with an annealing schedule for
the repeated-failure penalty weight $`w_{f}`$. Stronger penalties early
in training are intended to discourage repeatedly unsuccessful retrieval
actions and stabilize search behaviors, while weaker penalties later
allow more exploration.

| \Block 2-1Method | \Block 2-1Long Context Management | \Block \[c\]1-2Credit Assignment |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  |  Form of credits |  Source of credits |
|  GRPO |  – |  – |  – |
|  GiGPO |  – |  Advantage reweighting |  Successful and failed rollouts |
|  SUPO |  Summary |  – |  – |
|  ECHO |  Turn Selection |  Turn masking |  Successful rollouts only |
|  Self-Credit |  Summary |  Advantage reweighting |  Successful and failed rollouts |

Table 1: Key differences between Self-Credit and baseline methods.
Self-Credit leverages self-generated summaries during training to
provide credit assignment via advantage reweighting that is grounded in
both successful and failed rollouts via intra-group rescaling.

## 4 Experimental Setup

### 4.1 Setup

#### Task

We evaluate our method on the following long-horizon multi-hop QA and
deep research tasks: (1) BrowseComp-Plus ([Chen et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib37)): LLM agents interact with a search engine and
retrieve documents to solve multi-hop questions; (2) Deep research
tasks: we evaluate on GAIA ([Mialon et al., 2024](#bib.bib43)) and
xBench-DeepSearch ([Chen et al., 2025a](#bib.bib60)). These tasks
include real-world questions requiring multi-step reasoning, web
browsing, and tool use. For GAIA, we use its text-only subset.

#### Models

We train Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib54)), and
Gemma4-E4B ([Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)) with thinking mode.

#### Training

For BrowseComp-Plus, we follow [Xie et al. (2026)](#bib.bib42) and split
the dataset into 747 training examples for RL training and 83 test
examples for evaluation. We use the BrowseComp-Plus static corpus and
index as the search backend. For deep research tasks, we train on 1K
deep research QA pairs from OpenResearcher ([Li et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib45)) and use the OpenResearcher static browser as the
tool use harness and search backend during training. For efficient
training, we use a fully asynchronous rollout with VeRL ([Sheng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib55)) and Megatron ([Shoeybi et al., 2019](#bib.bib56))
frameworks. For Self-Credit, we use $`\tau_{+}=\tau_{-}=2`$ in all
experiments. Details can be found under
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Training Configurations ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").

### 4.2 Baselines

We compare against the following zero-shot and agentic RL baselines. The
main differences between Self-Credit and these baselines can be found in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.4 Annealing the Weights ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").
(1) Zero-shot evaluation of the base model does not use context
management; (2) GRPO is applied to the multi-turn setting without any
context management or turn-level credit assignment; (3) GiGPO ([Feng et
al., 2025](#bib.bib58)) modifies group-based RL with turn-level credit
assignment by re-grouping the same rollouts based on action states that
are matched by repetitive actions. Turns sharing an identical
environment observation are matched into groups, and within each group
the action receives a standardized additive advantage adjustment; (4)
SUPO ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)) is a compaction-augmented RL
baseline that implements a rolling summarization with a free-form
summary and optimizes the uniform-credit objective. There is no citation
instruction in the summarization prompt and no turn-level credit
assignment; (5) ECHO ([Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)) replaces free-form
summarization in summarization-augmented RL with explicit turn
selection: at each summarization, the policy emits a selection over its
turn history, and the selected turn memories are carried into the next
context in place of a summary. It routes token-level credit to the turns
selected by the policy in successful rollouts.

### 4.3 Evaluation Protocol

For BrowseComp-Plus, we follow [Chen et al. (2025b)](#bib.bib37); [Xie
et al. (2026)](#bib.bib42) and use the Qwen3-Embedding-8B ([Zhang et
al., 2025b](#bib.bib57)) retriever and the BrowseComp-Plus static corpus
index as the search engine during evaluation. We report LLM-as-a-judge
accuracy, prompting a separate Qwen3-32B judge to determine whether the
model-generated answer is semantically equivalent to the ground-truth
answer. For deep research tasks, we follow [Li et al.
(2026c)](#bib.bib45) to use open web search API instead of the static
engine during evaluation. We report LLM-as-a-judge accuracy as well with
the rubric from [Gupta et al. (2026)](#bib.bib59). For both tasks, we
use temperature = 0.7 for decoding.

|----|----|----|----|----|

Figure 3: Training dynamics on BrowseComp-Plus on Qwen3-32B models of RL

Self-Credit outperforms strong RL baselines across settings.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
reports test accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus. Self-Credit outperforms all
baselines at both Qwen3 model scales and beats the strongest baseline by
$`5.6`$ points at 32B and $`8.5`$ points at 8B.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
summarizes results on deep research tasks by training a Gemma4-E4B
model. On GAIA, Self-Credit achieves the highest accuracy and
outperforms the strongest baseline by $`4.9`$ points. On
xBench-DeepSearch, Self-Credit outperforms the best baseline by $`4.7`$
points. We also show that Self-Credit trains models that generalize
better to OOD shorter horizon search QA datasets in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D OOD Generalization ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").
These results demonstrate consistent gains across the evaluated model
families and benchmarks with Self-Credit.

Self-Credit learns efficient long-horizon tool use. Training dynamics of
different methods on BrowseComp-Plus shows the strength of Self-Credit
from balancing depth and efficiency of tool use for long horizon tasks.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
shows later in training, Self-Credit typically uses fewer turns than
ECHO does, while attaining high training reward. GRPO and GiGPO generate
much shorter trajectories and exhibit lower training reward. This
suggests that simply minimizing or maximizing interaction length for
long-horizon tasks is insufficient ([Yin et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)).
Together, these results show that Self-Credit supports sufficient
exploration to gather useful evidence while limiting excessive
interaction.

## 6 Analysis

### 6.1 Ablations

| \rectanglecolormetabg3-13-3 \rectanglecolormetabg7-17-3   | Qwen3-32B | Qwen3-8B |
|----|----|----|
| Self-Credit | 47.0 | 40.6 |
| Ablations on *Form of Credits* |  |  |
| –w/o Intra-group rescaling | 41.0 | 28.9 |
| –w/o Penalties for repeated failures | 34.9 | 26.5 |
| –w/o Rescaling for mixed outcomes | 41.0 | 31.3 |
| Ablations on *Source of Credits* |  |  |
| –w/o Self-generated citations | 42.2 | 27.7 |
| –w/ Random citations | 38.6 | 32.5 |

Table 4: Ablations of Self-Credit on BrowseComp-Plus. Intra-group
rescaling, penalties for repeated failures, and self-generated credits
are important for the downstream performance using Self-Credit.

To isolate the importance of different components of Self-Credit, we
conduct an ablation analysis with the following variants: (1) without
intra-group rescaling: we train models to summarize with citations and
*upweight* the advantages of all cited turns in rollouts with positive
advantages; (2) without penalties for repeated failures; (3) without
rescaling for mixed outcomes; (4) without self-generated citations: we
apply intra-group rescaling and advantage reweighting to *all turns*
instead of only the model-cited turns; (5) with random citations: we
apply intra-group rescaling and advantage reweighting to a random set of
turns in every segment, averaged over 3 seeds.

| \rectanglecolormetabg6-26-6 \rectanglecolormetabg11-211-6    |  |  Gold Searched (%) |  Gold Opened (%) |  Answer Recall (%) |  Evidence Recall (%) |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Qwen3-32B | GRPO |  42.2 |  25.3 |  33.9 |  29.5 |
|  | GiGPO |  42.2 |  12.0 |  25.1 |  25.3 |
|  | SUPO |  53.0 |  25.3 |  43.2 |  39.6 |
|  | ECHO |  62.7 |  30.1 |  51.6 |  48.3 |
|  | Self-Credit |  66.3 |  49.4 |  53.8 |  47.0 |
| Qwen3-8B | GRPO |  42.2 |  25.3 |  28.0 |  25.1 |
|  | GiGPO |  34.9 |  0.0 |  19.2 |  16.9 |
|  | SUPO |  42.2 |  9.6 |  30.4 |  27.8 |
|  | ECHO |  48.2 |  27.7 |  36.0 |  31.7 |
|  | Self-Credit |  50.6 |  32.5 |  36.7 |  32.0 |

Table 5: Analysis of the quality of tool use on BrowseComp-Plus for
different training methods. Gold Searched and Gold Opened measure the
percentage of questions for which at least one gold document appears
among the search results or is opened, respectively. Answer Recall and
Evidence Recall measure the fractions of documents containing the gold
answer or supporting evidence that are found through search or page
opening.

Table [4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 6.1 Ablations ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
summarizes the performance of these variants on BrowseComp-Plus. Among
the intra-group components, rescaling repeated turns in failed rollouts
is especially important for both model scales. Removing it reduces
accuracy from $`47.0\%`$ to $`34.9\%`$ for Qwen3-32B and from $`40.6\%`$
to $`26.5\%`$ for Qwen3-8B. We observe that without penalties for
repeated turns cited by failed rollouts, Qwen3-8B model learns to search
excessively, likely caused by over-optimizing for the credit boost, and
fails to learn to commit to an answer. Moreover, applying credit
assignment to all turns or randomly selected turns reduces Qwen3-8B
accuracy to $`27.7\%`$ and $`32.5\%`$, respectively, showing that
self-generated citations provide a better basis for credit assignment
than using arbitrary turns.

Overall, these results show that the different components of Self-Credit
work together: both self-generated citations and intra-group rescaling,
especially over repeated failures, are important for achieving the best
performance.

### 6.2 Quality of Credit Assignment

| \rectanglecolormetabg5-25-5 \rectanglecolormetabg9-29-5    |  | Opened | Searched | Judge F1 |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Qwen3-32B | Random | 18.2 | 32.8 | 44.7 |
|  | Cite all | 21.2 | 43.1 | 60.1 |
|  | ECHO | 40.7 | 39.7 | 60.6 |
|  | Self-Credit | 36.0 | 59.7 | 71.7 |
| Qwen3-8B | Random | 22.6 | 32.6 | 41.3 |
|  | Cite all | 26.9 | 41.4 | 53.9 |
|  | ECHO | 27.7 | 37.4 | 62.4 |
|  | Self-Credit | 45.7 | 58.1 | 69.3 |

Table 6: Quality of citations generated by different credit assignment
methods on BrowseComp-Plus. *Opened* and *Searched* report F1 (%)
between cited turns and turns whose *Open* or *Search* actions find gold
documents. *Judge F1* reports F1 (%) against turns judged relevant by a
stronger LLM judge.

Figure 4: Firing rate and precision of Self-Credit intra-group rescaling
across the three rules at different training stages on BrowseComp-Plus.
*Firing rate* denotes how frequently intra-group rescaling is applied to
a cited turn, and *firing precision* indicates whether rescaling gives
the correct credit to the cited turns. Intra-group rescaling is
triggered selectively during training for different models.

Self-Credit improves agentic tool use. We evaluate the quality of
agentic tool use of models trained using different methods on
BrowseComp-Plus, with a focus on two main types of tool use in this
task: *Search* and *Open*. Details of the evaluation metrics are in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Details of Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").
Table [5](#S6.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 6.1 Ablations ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
summarizes the results. Models trained with Self-Credit achieve higher
Gold Searched, Gold Opened, and Answer Recall scores than the baselines
at both model sizes.

Self-Credit generates better citations. To assess the quality of
citations generated by different methods, we evaluate whether the cited
turns perform actions that find gold documents for the agentic tasks. On
BrowseComp-Plus, we use *Open* or *Search* actions that find gold
documents as a proxy for critical actions, and we compute the F1 score
of cited turns against the turns containing such actions. We also
compute F1 against the important turn judged by Claude-4.6-Sonnet.
Details of the evaluation metrics are in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Details of Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").
Table [6](#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 6.2 Quality of Credit Assignment ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
reports the results for ECHO and Self-Credit; for reference, we
introduce a random citation baseline that cites a subset of all turns in
the rollout uniformly at random, and a baseline that cites all turns.
Self-Credit achieves higher citation quality than ECHO and baselines for
multiple metrics, especially better at identifying critical search
turns. This indicates Self-Credit trains a better policy at finding the
important turns in its generated rollouts, leading to a more reliable
source for credit assignment.

Intra-group rescaling is applied selectively and accurately. We evaluate
how frequently the intra-group rescaling is applied to cited turns
during the early (0–60 steps) and late (60–115 steps) training stages on
BrowseComp-Plus. We also report the precision of rescaling by checking
whether it gives extra credit to actions that are related to the gold
document, and reduces extra credit or give penalties for other less
relevant actions. Details of the evaluation metrics are in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Details of Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").
Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.2 Quality of Credit Assignment ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling")
shows that intra-group rescaling is triggered selectively. Compared with
a random selection baseline, Self-Credit provides higher quality
learning signals with high precision of crediting the good turns and
downweighting or penalizing the other turns.

## 7 Related Work

#### Agentic RL for long-horizon tasks.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used to post-train LLM agents
([Jin et al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Singh et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Qian
et al., 2025](#bib.bib22); [Wang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib21)), building
on policy-gradient methods such as PPO ([Schulman et al.,
2017](#bib.bib39)) and GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib40)). In
long-horizon tasks ([Sun et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)), growing interaction
histories can exceed the context window, while sparse outcome rewards
provide limited information about the contribution of individual actions
([Wang and Ammanabrolu, 2025](#bib.bib2); [Tang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)). Recent work addresses these challenges by using
inference-time methods ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Ye et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)), incorporating context management systems ([Li et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib48); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib24); [Kang et
al., 2026](#bib.bib25); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib26)) or
self-compaction capability ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib41); [Li et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib47); [Cursor Research et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)) into the
policy model through RL. Our work leverages self-compaction for context
management during training for long horizon tasks.

#### Credit assignment under sparse outcome rewards.

Prior work derives finer grained credit given sparse outcome rewards
from several sources, including learned critics ([Zhou et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7); [Shen et al., 2026](#bib.bib5); [Zhang et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib35); [Shi et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)), process reward
models ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib51); [Zeng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib36); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)), hindsight information
conditioned on answers ([Tan et al., 2026](#bib.bib50); [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib51)) and sampling ([Choudhury, 2025](#bib.bib49); [Zong
et al., 2026](#bib.bib53)), but these methods usually require additional
rollouts or hindsight information not available in intermediate steps.
Other methods reuse sampled rollouts to compare returns at similar
states ([Feng et al., 2025](#bib.bib58); [He et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)),
or leverage confidence of the policy model ([Wang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib52); [Dong et al., 2025](#bib.bib8); [Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib9)). Compared with prior work, our method combines
signals that exist in standard group-based RL methods with
self-compaction and rescales them using group-level statistics.

## 8 Conclusion

Training long-horizon LLM agents with RLVR is challenging because
outcome rewards provide very sparse learning signals over long
trajectories. We introduced Self-Credit, an end-to-end agentic RL method
that creates dense supervision signals from a single sparse outcome
reward through self-generated credit with intra-group rescaling. The
policy model generates summaries with citations to critical turns during
compaction, and these citations serve as self-generated credit.
Self-Credit then refines this credit with intra-group rescaling, which
compares cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the
same prompt, and uses the rescaled credit weights to selectively
strengthen the advantages of tokens in model-cited turns. Self-Credit
outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines on challenging search QA
and deep research tasks across models. These results suggest that
self-generated signals can be utilized for effective credit assignment
in long-horizon agentic RL.

## Appendix A Formulation Details

### A.1 GRPO Formulation

The advantage in GRPO is formulated as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{A}^{\,j}=\frac{R^{j}-\mean\big(\{R^{j^{\prime}}\}_{j^{\prime}=1}^{G}\big)}{\std\big(\{R^{j^{\prime}}\}_{j^{\prime}=1}^{G}\big)+\epsilon},\quad j\in\{1,\dots,G\},
``` |  | (5) |

where $`\epsilon>0`$ is a small constant for numerical stability.

The GRPO objective is defined as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\Biggl[\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{G}|\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}|}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}|}\min\Bigl(\rho^{j}_{\ell}\widehat{A}^{\,j},\quad\clip\bigl(\rho^{j}_{\ell},1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\bigr)\widehat{A}^{\,j}\Bigr)\Biggr],
``` |  | (6) |

where $`\rho^{j}_{\ell}`$ is the token-level importance ratio for the
$`\ell`$-th token in $`\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}`$.

#### Importance sampling ratio in GRPO.

Importance sampling ratio is the ratio of its probability under
$`M_{\theta}`$ to that under $`M_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}`$, both
conditioned on the context used to generate that token. Although
token-level importance ratios and clipping can produce different
gradient contributions, they do not provide turn-specific credit based
on each action’s contribution to the outcome.

## Appendix B Implementation Details

### B.1 Prompts and Instructions

The summarization instruction used in our experiments is the following.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Citation format.

We introduce simple format gating on the generated citations: the
citation line cannot be empty, and we strip out-of-range citations. An
invalid citation line leads to a format error and makes the entire
rollout receive a reward of 0.

#### Summary for the final segment.

Because compaction is only triggered at certain thresholds, turns in a
short last segment might not get a chance to be cited, creating a
systematic bias in the credit signal. Therefore, when a rollout
trajectory is complete with a final answer, we force the model to
generate an auxiliary summary of the final segment. This auxiliary
summary is not a context-replacing summary and is not included in
$`N^{j}`$.

### B.2 Turn Matching

#### Matching turns across rollouts by actions.

Intra-group rescaling requires deciding when a cited turn in one rollout
performs the same action as a turn in other rollouts for the same
prompt. As defined in
Section [2](#S2 "2 Preliminaries ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling"),
a turn consists of thinking trace, an agentic action, and an observation
from the environment. For the setting of long horizon agentic tasks, we
focus on *actions* to match turns because LLM agents learn to perform
the right actions during training. In the two settings below, instead of
comparing the text of tool calls, which rarely repeats verbatim across
rollouts, we identify each action by the *evidence it retrieves* from
the environment.

#### BrowseComp-Plus.

On BrowseComp-Plus, the agent interacts with a fixed document corpus
through three tools: (1) Search takes a natural-language query and
returns a ranked list of retrieved documents, each of which has a
document identifier (docid); (2) open_page takes a docid and returns the
full text of that document; (3) finish submits the final answer and ends
the interaction. We do not match turns with finish calls. For turns that
leverage the other 2 types of tools, we use the following matching
rules: (1) A search call is represented by the set of docids it
returned. Within each prompt group, we match search turns by the overlap
between the sets of retrieved docids. Two turns are matched if the
Jaccard similarity of their sets of retrieved docids is at least
$`0.6`$; (2) For open_page, we match turns by the docid they opened ,
and two open_page turns match only if they opened the same document.

#### Deep research tasks.

For deep research tasks, the agent browses a fixed web corpus with
OpenResearch harness during training through four tools: (1) search
takes a natural-language query and returns the top 20 results as links;
(2) open takes a link id or cursor from an earlier observation and
returns the page content with line numbers; (3) find takes a text
pattern and returns the lines in an opened page that match it; (4)
finish submits the final answer and ends the interaction. Unlike on
BrowseComp-Plus, the agent refers to pages through link ids (e.g., URLs)
and cursors (location on the website) that are local to each rollout,
making matching harder. Therefore, we identify each document by its
docid in the OpenResearcher corpus, which the retriever returns as
metadata hidden from the agent, instead of by links or cursors. As in
BrowseComp-Plus, we do not match turns with finish calls, and we match
search turns by the Jaccard similarity of their retrieved docids (at
least $`0.6`$) and open turns by the docid they opened. For find, two
turns match if they found adjacent lines in the same document.

#### Turn matching for other tasks.

The matching rules above are instances of a general recipe: a
task-specific function matches turns by the observations from those
turns. Intra-group rescaling only needs these matches, so it can be
applied unchanged to other agentic tasks once such a function is
defined. This recipe is related to anchor-state grouping in GiGPO ([Feng
et al., 2025](#bib.bib58)), which groups steps across trajectories that
start from the same environment state, using exact matching or a
similarity threshold over the state text. The difference lies in what is
matched: GiGPO compares the states in which actions are taken, while
Self-Credit compares the observations that cited actions obtain, which
remains informative in open-ended environments where states rarely
repeat. For example, in embodied tasks such as ALFWorld ([Shridhar et
al., 2021](#bib.bib11)), a turn can be described by the object and
receptacle it acts on (e.g., an object picked by the agent), together
with whether the action succeeded.

#### Independence Assumption

In this work, we assume that different turns in a rollout contribute
independently to the outcome, which is an approximation: an open action
depends on the search that surfaced the document, and a late turn may
only succeed because of evidence gathered earlier. We adopt the
approximation because it keeps the comparison to counts over rollouts
rather than over trajectory prefixes, which would rarely match.

## Appendix C Training Configurations

### C.1 General Hyperparameters

Following [Xie et al. (2026)](#bib.bib42); [Li et al.
(2026c)](#bib.bib45), we use the same training configuration on
BrowseComp-Plus and deep research tasks for all training methods,
including Self-Credit:

- •
  Optimization. We use a learning rate of $`1\times 10^{-6}`$ with a
  constant schedule and asymmetric clipping with
  $`\epsilon_{\text{low}}=0.20`$ and $`\epsilon_{\text{high}}=0.28`$.
  The loss is averaged over tokens, with no entropy bonus, no KL penalty
  in either the loss or the reward, and no critic.
- •
  Batching. Each training step uses 256 trajectories, split into 8
  optimizer updates. We use $`16`$ prompts per step and $`16`$ rollouts
  per prompt.
- •
  Sequence lengths. The maximum prompt length is 4096 tokens and the
  maximum response length is 32768 tokens. The threshold for compaction
  is 16384 tokens.
- •
  Rollouts. Rollouts are generated asynchronously in a multi-turn agent
  loop, with tool calls in the Hermes format. Tool responses are
  truncated to 16K characters. The maximum number of assistant turns is
  100.

  For BrowseComp-Plus, we allow the model to use 5 parallel tool calls
  and train for 115 steps, following the settings used by [Xie et al.
  (2026)](#bib.bib42). For deep research tasks, we allow the model to
  use 1 parallel tool call. We train for 100 steps. All training runs
  are conducted on 8x8 NVIDIA B200 GPU.

### C.2 Hyperparameters of Baselines

We use the official implementations of the baseline methods.

#### ECHO.

We set turn-selection top-k to $`5`$ and keep $`3`$ recent turns
verbatim.

#### GiGPO.

We use discount $`\gamma=0.95`$. Turns are grouped by similarity of the
raw observation texts, as implemented by the original GiGPO paper.

### C.3 Hyperparameters of Self-Credit

For all models on both datasets, we set maximum number of summary rounds
to 10, $`\beta=1.5`$, $`w_{s}=2.5`$, and $`w_{f}=1.5`$, annealed to
$`w_{f}=1.0`$ linearly.

## Appendix D OOD Generalization

|             | HotpotQA | MuSiQue | FRAMES | Bamboogle | Avg. |
|-------------|----------|---------|--------|-----------|------|
| GRPO        | 64.5     | 29.4    | 48.4   | 39.2      | 45.4 |
| GiGPO       | 63.2     | 31.6    | 51.7   | 32.0      | 44.6 |
| SUPO        | 63.7     | 30.6    | 47.8   | 35.2      | 44.3 |
| ECHO        | 63.4     | 31.8    | 49.2   | 33.6      | 44.5 |
| Self-Credit | 65.1     | 28.0    | 51.7   | 41.6      | 46.6 |

Table 7: Zero-shot generalization on out-of-distribution
search-augmented QA tasks.

### D.1 Out-of-distribution Generalization

To evaluate the out-of-distribution transfer of different methods to
shorter horizon tasks after training on long horizon, we evaluate
zero-shot transfer of the Qwen3-32B policies to four out-of-distribution
search-augmented QA benchmarks, following prior work ([Jin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib20); [Xie et al., 2026](#bib.bib42)). As shown in
Table [7](#A4.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Appendix D OOD Generalization ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling"),
Self-Credit achieves the highest average accuracy, $`46.6\%`$, compared
with $`45.4\%`$ for GRPO, $`44.5\%`$ for ECHO, and $`44.3\%`$ for SUPO.
This demonstrates that tool use behaviors learned with long horizon
training with Self-Credit generalize to shorter tasks as well.

## Appendix E Details of Analysis

#### Tool-use quality metrics.

BrowseComp-Plus annotates each question with gold documents, which
contain the answer, and a larger set of evidence documents, which are
needed to support it. *Gold Searched* and *Gold Opened* are the
percentages of questions for which at least one gold document appeared
in any search result or was opened, respectively. *Answer Recall* is the
fraction of a question’s gold documents that the policy either retrieved
or opened, averaged over questions, and *Evidence Recall* is the same
quantity computed over evidence documents.

#### Citation quality metrics in Table [6](#S6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 6.2 Quality of Credit Assignment ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").

\(1\) *Opened* and *Searched*. We measure whether the turns a model
cites contain the evidence needed for the answer, using the gold
documents that BrowseComp-Plus annotates in the dataset. An Open or
Search turn is considered important if it opened a gold document
(*Opened*) or if one of its search results was a gold document
(*Searched*). We compute the F1 of the cited turns against these turns,
excluding the final answer turn. (2) *LLM Judge.* A useful exploratory
turn may not find any gold documents but still inform the model about
what to do next. While these turns still provide learning signals, the
metrics above might overlook such turns. Therefore, we use *LLM Judge*
F1 to score model citations against turns that Claude Sonnet 4.6 labels
as decisive or as finding new relevant information, which does not rely
on gold annotations. We use the LLM-as-judge prompt from [Xu et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib1).

#### Rule firing and precision in Figure [4](#S6.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 6.2 Quality of Credit Assignment ‣ 6 Analysis ‣ Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling").

We measure how often each intra-group rescaling rule scenario is applied
during training and whether it is applied to the right turns. The
*firing rate* is the fraction of cited turns on which a rule is applied.
The *firing precision* checks fired turns against turns that find the
gold documents, i.e., turns that either opened a gold document or if one
of its search results was a gold document. For the repeated success
scenario, the firing precision is the share of fired turns that find
gold documents. For repeated failure and mixed outcome, its precision is
the share of fired turns that do not find gold documents.
````
